subject: Copywriting
title: Headlines Carry Everything
description: A fast breakdown of Headlines Carry Everything for builders.

hook.text: Ogilvy said five times as many people read the headline as the body.

buildup.text: Every legend invested disproportionate time on headlines.

discovery.text: The headline does the heavy lifting: it grabs attention, promises a benefit, and selects the right audience.

twist.text: In digital, the headline IS the ad. A tweet, a subject line, a Google ad—all headlines competing for one click.

climax.text: If the headline fails, nothing else matters. Body copy, design, and price are irrelevant to someone who never clicked.

punchline.text: Headline fails, nothing else matters. Write it last, perfect it first.

quiz.question: According to Ogilvy, how many more people read the headline vs body copy?

details.summary: Across the careers of every copywriting legend, one lesson is universal: the headline is the most important element of any piece of copy. Five times more people read headlines than body copy. A brilliant headline with mediocre body copy will outperform a brilliant body with a mediocre headline...
details.whyItMatters: If the headline fails, nothing else matters. This lesson — validated by Caples, Ogilvy, Schwartz, and every major copywriter — is the single most important tactical principle in the craft.
takeaways: Five times more people read headlines than body copy
Ogilvy said writing the headline spends 80 cents of every ad dollar
Headline testing produces the largest performance gains in copy

faq.question: Why do headlines matter more than body copy?
faq.answer: Most people scan rather than read. If the headline does not capture attention and promise value, the body copy is never read — no matter how brilliant it is. The headline is the ad for the ad. It must earn the next line of reading.

faq.question: What makes a headline effective?
faq.answer: Effective headlines promise a specific benefit, target a clear audience, and create curiosity or urgency. Testing repeatedly shows that headlines with numbers, 'how to' promises, or direct benefit statements outperform clever or abstract alternatives.
